text: Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters in front of DispatcherServlet; for APIs I go stateless with JWT validation, and 401 means unauthenticated while 403 means forbidden. **Filters** run *before* DispatcherServlet: authentication, CORS, request logging. **HandlerInterceptors** run around a controller call and know which handler was chosen. Spring Security is a **SecurityFilterChain**. Authentication = *who are you*; authorization = *what may you do*. Stateless APIs validate a **JWT** on every request; no server session. **401** = not authenticated. **403** = authenticated, but not allowed.

title: The test pyramid
text: I keep a wide base of fast unit tests, a focused layer of integration tests against real infrastructure, and only a few end-to-end tests for critical journeys. **Unit tests**: one class, dependencies mocked, milliseconds each. **Integration tests**: real Spring wiring and a real database (Testcontainers). **Contract tests** check that services agree on their APIs (Spring Cloud Contract, Pact). **End-to-end tests**: few, slow, flaky-prone — keep them to the critical journeys. Good tests are **FIRST**: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely. Structure them as *given / when / then*.

title: JUnit 5 essentials
text: In JUnit 5 I use parameterized tests to cover many inputs, assertThrows for failure paths and assertAll when one scenario has several checks. `@Test`, `@BeforeEach` / `@AfterEach`, `@BeforeAll` / `@AfterAll` (static by default), `@DisplayName`, `@Nested`, `@Disabled`. `assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, **`assertThrows`**, `assertAll` (reports every failure together), `assertTimeout`. **`@ParameterizedTest`** with `@ValueSource`, `@CsvSource` or `@MethodSource` — one test, many inputs. JUnit 5 = **Platform** (runs tests) + **Jupiter** (the new API) + **Vintage** (runs JUnit 4 tests). AssertJ's `assertThat(x).isEqualTo(y)` reads better and fails with clearer messages.

title: Mockito: mocks, spies & verify
text: A mock returns defaults until stubbed, while a spy wraps a real object and runs real code unless stubbed; I stub with when/thenReturn, use doReturn for spies, and verify the interactions that matter. **mock()**: every method returns a default — `0`, `false`, `null`, an empty collection — until you stub it. Stub with `when(x.call()).thenReturn(...)` or `thenThrow(...)`. Check interactions with `verify(x, times(1)).call()` and `never()`. **spy()** wraps a real object: **real methods run** unless stubbed. Stub a spy with **`doReturn(v).when(spy).call()`** — `when(spy.call())` runs the real method while you're still setting up. `@Mock` + `@InjectMocks` with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`. Capture arguments with `ArgumentCaptor`.

title: @SpringBootTest vs test slices
text: I test controllers with @WebMvcTest and MockMvc, repositories with @DataJpaTest, and keep @SpringBootTest for a few end-to-end integration tests, because slices are faster and more focused. **@SpringBootTest** loads the full context — for integration tests, often with `webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT`. **@WebMvcTest(Controller.class)** loads only the MVC layer (controllers, advice, filters, converters) and gives you **MockMvc**. Services are replaced with `@MockitoBean`. **@DataJpaTest** loads JPA repositories, and **rolls back after each test**. Other slices: `@JsonTest`, `@RestClientTest`, `@WebFluxTest`. Spring caches contexts between tests; a different set of mock beans means a new context, which is slow.

title: Testcontainers
text: I run repository and integration tests against real infrastructure with Testcontainers and @ServiceConnection, because an in-memory database hides dialect and locking differences. H2's SQL dialect differs from Postgres and MySQL (JSONB, native queries, locking), so bugs hide until production. Testcontainers runs **real** Postgres, Kafka, Redis and more in throwaway Docker containers. Spring Boot 3.1+ **`@ServiceConnection`** wires connection details from the container automatically. Share one static container across tests for speed, and run your Flyway or Liquibase migrations against it.

title: TDD & code coverage
text: TDD is red, green, refactor; I read JaCoCo coverage as a map of untested branches rather than a target, because coverage proves code ran, not that it was checked. **Red → green → refactor**, in small loops. TDD pushes you towards testable design and leaves a safety net behind for every change. **JaCoCo** measures line and branch coverage (`mvn verify`, then `target/site/jacoco`), and can fail the build under a threshold. Coverage measures *execution*, not *verification*: a test with no assertions still covers lines. **Mutation testing** (PIT) plants small bugs and checks whether your tests notice.
